warn.label: Amber
warn.text: Usable with care. The reason says what to watch.

not_in_export.label: Not in export
not_in_export.text: The export doesn't contain this. Not a judgement on your system.

needs_human.label: Needs a human
needs_human.text: Can't be judged automatically. The report says what to look at.

too_few.label: Too few to judge
too_few.text: The column holds some values, but too few to judge anything from. The reason says how many it found.

owner.label: Owner
owner.means: who the case is assigned to
owner.unlocks: the routing-quality check B1, and the per-owner signals once history or an owner count is present

group.label: Group or queue
group.means: the team or queue holding the case
group.unlocks: routing quality B1, the escalation cross-check B7, and the by-group breakdown in the slow-cases and open-work signals

reason.label: Contact reason
reason.means: why the customer got in touch
reason.unlocks: every theme question: catch-all share B2, near-duplicate reasons B3, team-type reasons AI2, theme movers, self-help and keep-a-human

subject.label: Subject
subject.unlocks: usable customer wording AI1, and the billing churn driver

account_id.label: Account
account_id.means: which customer the case belongs to
account_id.unlocks: account linkage B9, and every churn driver, none of which can run without cases grouped by account

account_size.label: Account size
account_size.means: the account's size, plan or tier band
account_size.unlocks: stratification B10, so case volume can be told apart from a real churn driver

segment.label: Product or segment
segment.unlocks: stratification B10, and it is preferred over account size as the churn control

channel.label: Channel
channel.unlocks: the email and chat volume estimate AI6, and the phone-contact churn driver

reopen_count.label: Reopens
reopen_count.means: how many times the case was reopened
reopen_count.unlocks: reopen history C2 and B6, and the reopened-case churn driver

follow_up_of.label: Follow-up of
follow_up_of.unlocks: repeat contact after closure B6, which reopen counts on their own miss

escalated.label: Escalated flag
escalated.unlocks: the escalation-flag check B7, which holds the flag up against what history shows

owner_changes.label: Owners count
owner_changes.means: how many owners the case passed through
owner_changes.unlocks: counts-only history C2, and the handoff and slow-and-passed-around signals where there is no change log

group_changes.label: Groups count
group_changes.means: how many teams or queues the case passed through

wait_time.label: Customer wait time
wait_time.means: time the case spent waiting on the customer
wait_time.unlocks: the resolution-time caveat B5, which says whether slow really means slow

resolution_note.label: Resolution note
resolution_note.unlocks: the solution-record check AI4, and the documented share on self-help candidates

linked_article.label: Linked article
linked_article.means: the knowledge article or macro used

last_update_at.label: Last update
last_update_at.unlocks: the open-work-at-risk signal; derived from the latest public comment when no column carries it

csat_score.label: CSAT score
csat_score.means: the survey score the customer gave
csat_score.unlocks: survey coverage B8, the CSAT column on the handoff signal, and the low-CSAT churn driver

churned.label: Churned
churned.unlocks: every churn driver; without an outcome column no case pattern can be tested against one

exit_event.label: Exit event
exit_event.means: a cancellation or similar event logged on the case
exit_event.unlocks: the exit-events signal, for whoever owns retention

comment_id.label: Comment ID
comment_id.unlocks: an exact comment count: without one, two short replies sent in the same minute look like one row sent twice, so the counts are a floor

comment_body.label: Comment body
comment_body.unlocks: customer wording from the comments AI1, and the billing churn driver, in exports where the subject and description are empty

comment_at.label: Comment time
comment_at.unlocks: comment ordering, and the last-update derivation when no case column carries it

comment_author.label: Comment author
comment_author.unlocks: nothing yet: it is read and kept with each comment, but no check reads it

comment_author_type.label: Comment author type
comment_author_type.means: whether an agent or the customer wrote it
comment_author_type.unlocks: nothing yet: it is read and kept with each comment, but no check reads it

comment_public.label: Comment is public
comment_public.means: whether the customer could see the comment, true meaning public
comment_public.unlocks: a last update taken from the latest public comment rather than from an internal note

comment_private.label: Comment is internal
comment_private.means: whether the comment is an internal note, true meaning internal
comment_private.unlocks: the same question as comment is public, read the other way round

checks.title: Core columns are present
checks.metric: Share of the four core fields (case ID, created, closed, status) found in the export
checks.why: Case ID, opened, closed and status underpin every other check and signal.
checks.fix: Add the missing columns to the export. All major helpdesks have them as standard fields.

checks.title: Case history is available
checks.metric: History file present (green), count columns only (amber), neither (not in export)
checks.why: Without history you can't see transfers, reopens or how long cases sat with each team. Standard CSV exports usually leave it out.
checks.fix: In Zendesk, add ticket metrics fields or pull ticket audits through the API. In Salesforce, turn on field history for Owner and Status and export Case History.

checks.title: History covers the period analysed
checks.failure_title: History is shorter than the period analysed
checks.metric: Share of cases created after history tracking began
checks.why: Salesforce keeps field history for up to 18 months, and only from when tracking was switched on. Older cases look as if they never moved.
checks.fix: Limit analysis to the period history covers, or extend retention.

checks.title: Each case appears once
checks.warn_title: Some cases appear more than once
checks.conflict_title: A column mapped as a case field changes between comments
checks.conflict_fix: Map that column to a comment field instead, or leave it unmapped. If it really is a case field, find what writes a different value per comment row: the collapse keeps the first value it sees for each case and drops the rest.
checks.metric: One row per case: share of rows whose case ID appears more than once. One row per comment: share of cases whose case-level columns disagree between their rows.
checks.why: Two rows for one case inflate volume and distort every rate. A repeated case ID is only that, though, when the export is one row per case. An export with one row per comment or email repeats the case fields on every row by design: case uniqueness still holds once the rows are collapsed, so resolution time, counts and rates are unaffected, and the shape is named rather than failed. What can still go wrong there is a dirty collapse, where two rows of one case claim different owners or statuses and one of them has to be discarded. That is what this measures in a comment export.
checks.fix: In a one-row-per-case export, deduplicate on case ID and check whether the export joined a one-to-many table. In a one-row-per-comment export, nothing here needs fixing unless a case's rows disagree; then find what writes a case field per comment row, because the collapse keeps the first value and drops the rest.
checks.note: Rows identical in every column are dropped before this is measured, in either shape, and reported in what was read. In a one-row-per-case export they are also a repeated case ID, so they count here. In a one-row-per-comment export they do not: they often mean the export carries no comment ID or timestamp, so two short replies look identical, and that is a reason to treat the comment counts as a floor rather than to distrust the cases.

checks.title: Routing fields are genuinely filled
checks.failure_title: Routing fields are mostly empty or placeholders
checks.metric: Lowest real fill rate across owner, group and reason (placeholders like "N/A" and "Other" count as empty)
checks.why: A field that is mostly "N/A" or "Other" is empty in practice, however full it looks.
checks.fix: Make the field required at closure and remove placeholder defaults.

checks.title: Reasons aren't dominated by a catch-all
checks.failure_title: A catch-all reason swallows too many cases
checks.metric: Share of cases whose reason is blank or a catch-all such as "Other" or "General"
checks.why: Whatever sits in "Other" is invisible to reporting and to any AI trained on your reasons.
checks.fix: Sample the catch-all, split its biggest themes into new reasons, and remove "Other" as a default.
checks.note: Practitioner rules of thumb only. No research-grade threshold exists.

checks.title: Reason codes are a tidy set
checks.metric: Near-duplicate reason pairs (green none, amber up to 3) and share of reasons used fewer than 5 times
checks.why: Duplicates like "SSO" and "Single sign-on" split one issue in two and make trends meaningless.
checks.fix: Merge near-duplicates, retire rarely used values, and keep each level to a handful of options.

checks.title: Dates make sense
checks.metric: Share of cases closed before they were created, or with a status that contradicts the close date
checks.why: One bad date can wreck an average resolution time.
checks.fix: Find the automation or import writing bad dates, and exclude affected cases until fixed.

checks.title: Resolution time separates customer wait
checks.failure_title: Can't separate customer wait from agent work
checks.metric: A customer-wait or on-hold time field is present and filled
checks.why: Zendesk's full resolution time includes pending time and runs to the last solve. Without a wait field, "slow" may just mean "waiting on the customer".
checks.fix: Add requester-wait or on-hold time to the export.

checks.title: Reopens can be counted
checks.metric: Reopen count present (amber); plus follow-up cases linked to originals (green)
checks.why: In Zendesk, a reply to a closed ticket creates a new follow-up ticket instead of a reopen, so reopen counts miss repeat contacts.
checks.fix: Include the reopens metric and link follow-up tickets to their originals.

checks.title: The escalation flag is actually used
checks.failure_title: The escalation flag is rarely set
checks.metric: Share of cases flagged, compared with the share that history shows moving to engineering or tier 3
checks.why: A flag that's almost never set usually means nobody sets it, not that nothing happens.
checks.fix: Set the flag automatically from the routing event, or stop reporting on it.

checks.title: Survey scores are linked to cases
checks.failure_title: Few closed cases carry a survey score
checks.metric: Share of closed cases with a CSAT score
checks.why: Survey analysis needs enough linked responses, and the happiest customers answer most, so low coverage hides real gaps.
checks.fix: Link survey responses to case IDs; compare who responds with who doesn't before modelling.

checks.title: Cases link to accounts
checks.metric: Share of cases with a real account ID
checks.why: Churn analysis happens at account level. Unlinked cases drop out silently.
checks.fix: Require an account on every case, or match on contact email domain.

checks.title: You can control for account size or product
checks.metric: Account size or product/segment present and filled on 90% of cases
checks.why: Bigger, busier accounts raise more cases and behave differently. Without a size or segment field, every apparent driver is confounded.
checks.fix: Join account size band and product to the export.

checks.title: Customers' words are captured
checks.metric: Share of cases whose subject or description has five or more words and isn't a stock phrase
checks.why: Without the customer's own words you can't discover what they want, the first job of any AI self-help project.
checks.fix: Include the first customer message. Zendesk CSV exports leave out descriptions, so use JSON or the API.

checks.title: Reasons describe customer needs
checks.metric: Share of volume whose reason names a team, tier or process ("Tier 2", "Escalated")
checks.why: A reason like "Tier 2" tells a bot nothing about what the customer wanted. AI intents must describe the customer's need.
checks.fix: Keep routing in routing fields and rewrite reasons as customer needs.

checks.title: Reasons don't overlap
checks.metric: Reviewed by a person in this version; the report lists near-duplicate reasons to start from
checks.why: Zendesk warns that overlapping intents cause "low-confidence or wrong topic detection".
checks.fix: Merge or redefine overlapping reasons so each covers one need.

checks.title: Solutions are recorded
checks.failure_title: Few cases record how they were solved
checks.metric: Share of closed cases with a resolution note or linked article
checks.why: AI agents answer from written knowledge. If solutions live only in agents' heads, there's nothing to ground an answer in.
checks.fix: Require a resolution note or linked article at closure, and mine macros for missing articles.

checks.title: Demand is concentrated enough to automate
checks.failure_title: Demand is too scattered to automate easily
checks.metric: Share of cases with a real reason that fall in the ten most common reasons
checks.why: Automation pays back fastest on frequent, repeated questions.
checks.fix: Start with the top themes and leave the long tail to people.

checks.title: Volume meets published vendor minimums
checks.failure_title: Volume is below some vendors' published minimums
checks.metric: Total cases against Forethought's published 20,000+ historical tickets and 2,000+ email or chat tickets a month
checks.why: Some vendors need a minimum history to train. Most don't publish one, so ask.
checks.fix: Ask each vendor for its minimum before a pilot.

checks.title: Bot conversations can be linked to later cases
checks.failure_title: Bot conversations aren't linked to later cases
checks.warn_title: Bot conversations can only be matched by account and timing
checks.metric: Follow-up case IDs on each conversation (green); account plus conversation start and end times, so returns have to be matched (amber); neither in the export (not in export)
checks.why: The audit asks what happened after the bot claimed a resolution. Without a way to reach from a conversation to the cases that followed it, a claimed resolution can't be confirmed or contradicted, and silence can't be told apart from success.
checks.fix: Export the follow-up case IDs on each conversation. Failing that, export the account ID with the conversation's start and end times, which lets returns be matched by account and timing.

outcomes.pass: Each conversation carries the cases that followed it, so claimed resolutions can be checked directly.
outcomes.warn: Conversations carry an account and start and end times, but no case links. Matching returns by timing alone isn't supported yet, so this export can't be audited. Every claimed resolution is reported as can't tell; export the follow-up case IDs and the audit runs.
outcomes.not_in_export: This export doesn't contain the link between bot conversations and the cases that followed them. The link may well exist in your bot or your helpdesk; it isn't in these files.
outcomes.too_few: Nothing in this file is marked as a resolution the bot claimed, so there is nothing for the audit to check. A bot conversations export records whether the bot claimed it resolved each conversation; a file with none of those is probably not one, or the claimed-resolution column has not been mapped.
outcomes.same_file: This looks like the same file as the case export: same columns, same number of rows, same values where checked. The audit asks what happened in the cases *after* a bot conversation, so it needs the bot's own conversations, not the cases again.

checks.same_file_title: The bot file looks like the case file
checks.note: The engine reports these words verbatim, and uses warn_title on the amber path, because the account and the timings are present and "aren't linked" would misdescribe the export. Only the green path is implemented. Amber is a limit of this tool, not a flaw in the data, so the use reports "needs a human" rather than amber "usable with care".

signals.title: Slow and passed-around cases
signals.shows: Cases open more than 30 days with three or more owners, by group
signals.disclaimer: The one service signal worth watching. Not proof that it causes churn.

signals.title: Handed off versus held
signals.shows: Resolution time and CSAT for cases kept by one owner versus handed on
signals.disclaimer: Harder cases get handed on, so this isn't a fair comparison of teams.

signals.title: Theme movers
signals.shows: Reasons rising or falling in the last quarter against the previous nine months
signals.disclaimer: Shows what is moving, not why.

signals.title: Open work at risk
signals.shows: Open cases older than 70% of closed cases took to resolve
signals.disclaimer: Not a prediction of which customers will leave.

signals.title: Exit events
signals.shows: Cancellations and similar events logged in cases, for whoever owns retention
signals.disclaimer: A commercial warning recorded in support, not something support caused.

signals.title: AI self-help candidates
signals.shows: Reasons that are frequent, quick, single-owner and documented
signals.disclaimer: A shortlist to test, not a deflection forecast.

signals.title: Keep-a-human themes
signals.shows: Reasons with long resolution times or many owners
signals.disclaimer: Where automation is most likely to frustrate customers.

conflicting_case_field.title: A column mapped as a case field changes between comments
conflicting_case_field.text: This reads a field whose value differs between a case's own comment rows, so the collapse kept the first value and dropped the rest. Either that column holds a value per comment rather than per case, in which case map it to a comment field, or something writes it per row and the number here is built on one row's answer.

dropped_comment_rows.title: Comment rows were dropped as identical
dropped_comment_rows.text: Rows identical in every column were dropped before this was measured, so the comment counts are a floor rather than a count. This often means the export carries no comment ID or timestamp: two short replies sent at the same minute, such as "Thanks" twice, then look like one row sent twice. Dropping them changes no case: each is still there once, with the same dates, owner and reason.

resolution_audit.disclaimer: "Not contradicted" means silence, not success. It records only that no follow-up case appeared in the window: the customer may have given up, gone elsewhere, or left. Never report it as a resolution rate.

vendor_questions: How do you define a resolution, and how do you count reopens?
Do you report containment separately from resolution?
What minimum ticket history and monthly volume do you need?
Do you learn from our past tickets, our knowledge articles, or both?
What happens when our reasons or tags overlap?
Who grades the resolutions, you or us?
